content.title: About
content.content: Apple is the edible fruit of the apple tree (Malus domestica) that grows in temperate regions worldwide. Apples have a sweet‑tart flavor, crisp texture, and can be eaten raw or used in cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Apple is often regarded as a symbol of health and appears in many proverbs and stories.
There are over 7,500 apple varieties differing in taste, color, and harvest time.
Apple juice was the first beverage consumed by astronauts in space.
Apple skin contains more nutrients than the flesh.
In ancient Rome, apples were used as a remedy for cough.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber improves digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Antioxidant content
items.content: Flavonoids and polyphenols protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Potassium and soluble fiber contribute to normal blood pressure.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Apples provide energy with relatively few calories, making them diet‑friendly.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to apples.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Surface residues can remain on the skin; thorough washing or peeling is recommended.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: High fructose content may cause discomfort for people with sensitive stomachs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Apples can be eaten fresh, sliced into salads, made into compotes, juices, baked goods, and sauces. For a softer texture, they can be lightly boiled or baked.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store apples in a cool, dry place or refrigerate at 0‑4 °C. For long‑term storage keep them in a separate drawer to prevent them from affecting other fruits.

bread-wheat-or-cracked-wheat-with-raisin.title: Bread, wheat or cracked wheat with raisins

content.title: About
content.content: Bread made from whole wheat or cracked wheat with added raisins is a traditional baked product prepared from whole‑grain flour, water, yeast, and a small amount of sugar. Raisins give the loaf a sweet flavor, aromatic notes, and extra nutritional value.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Raisins have been used as a natural sweetener in bread since ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt.
Cracked wheat retains more fiber and minerals than refined flour.
Raisin bread is a common festive treat in Russia and many Eastern European countries.
The sugar in raisins helps accelerate dough fermentation.
The dark crust of this bread is caused by caramelization of raisin sugars.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain wheat and raisins provide soluble and insoluble fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The loaf contains thiamine, niacin, and folate, essential for metabolic processes.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Raisins are rich in polyphenols, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Wheat and raisins supply iron, magnesium, and potassium.

items.title: Energy‑dense
items.content: The combination of complex carbohydrates and natural sugars provides sustained satiety.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Raisins increase the overall sugar level, which may be a concern for people with diabetes.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Wheat‑based bread contains gluten and is unsuitable for individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Raisin allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to dried fruits.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raisin bread works well for breakfast, as a sandwich base, alongside soups, or as a snack. It can be toasted and spread with butter, cream cheese, or jam.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the loaf in a paper bag or cloth sack at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer keeping, place it in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to a week or freeze in portions.

content.title: About
content.content: Nonfat cheddar is a cheese made from skimmed cow’s milk. It retains the sharp flavor of traditional cheddar while containing virtually no fat (usually less than 0.5%). It is used in cooking when a strong cheese taste is desired without added calories.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cheddar originated in the English county of Somerset in the 12th century.
Nonfat cheddar often undergoes ultrafiltration to remove most of the milk fat.
The cheese can be aged from a few weeks to several years; longer aging intensifies flavor and creates a crumbly texture.
Cheddar melts consistently, making it a popular base for sauces and casseroles.
In the United States, nonfat cheddar is frequently listed in low‑fat diet recommendations.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Provides about 25 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Rich source of calcium
items.content: Contains over 700 mg of calcium per 100 g, important for bone health.

items.title: Very low fat
items.content: Less than 0.5 % fat makes it suitable for calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Supplies vitamin B12, riboflavin (B2) and niacin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Phosphorus and zinc
items.content: These minerals support cellular metabolism and immune function.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Although much of the lactose is removed, small amounts remain.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey may react to the cheese.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Nonfat cheddar is often salted; individuals monitoring sodium should watch portions.

items.title: Crystal formation
items.content: Long‑term storage can lead to calcium‑phosphate crystals that alter texture.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice nonfat cheddar for salads, add to sandwiches, use in casseroles, sauces and pizza. It grates well for topping dishes. For a softer texture, gently warm the cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in the original packaging or an airtight container in the refrigerator at +2–4 °C. Shelf life after opening is typically 4–6 weeks. Discard if you notice mold, off‑odors, or discoloration.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-cheese-.title: Egg omelet with cheese, tomatoes and dark‑green vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: An omelet made from eggs, enriched with cheese, tomatoes and dark‑green vegetables such as spinach or broccoli. It is a nutrient‑dense dish rich in protein, vitamins and minerals, suitable for breakfast or a light lunch.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are an excellent source of complete protein, containing all essential amino acids.
Cheese adds calcium and enhances flavor, increasing the dish’s energy value.
Dark‑green vegetables are high in lutein and zeaxanthin, which support eye health.
Tomatoes provide lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that becomes more bioavailable after cooking.
An omelet cooks quickly—usually 5‑7 minutes on the stovetop.

items.title: Muscle support
items.content: Egg protein aids muscle growth and repair, especially important for active individuals.

items.title: Bone health
items.content: Calcium from cheese and vitamin K from green vegetables help maintain bone density.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes and carotenoids from greens protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamins A, C and B‑complex present in the ingredients support normal immune function.

items.title: Sustained energy
items.content: The combination of protein, fat and carbohydrates provides lasting satiety and stable energy levels.

items.title: Egg or dairy allergy
items.content: People allergic to eggs or dairy proteins (casein) may experience reactions up to anaphylaxis.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Using salty cheese can raise the sodium level, which is undesirable for hypertension.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolks contain cholesterol; individuals with high cholesterol should consume in moderation.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked eggs may harbor Salmonella; ensure the omelet is fully cooked.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the omelet hot, optionally garnish with fresh herbs, add a slice of whole‑grain bread or avocado. It can be eaten with a fork or cut into wedges.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best enjoyed immediately. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours and reheat in a pan or microwave.

pasta-whole-grain-with-tomato-based-sauc.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Tomato Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pasta with tomato sauce is a dish made from whole‑grain pasta tossed in a fragrant sauce of ripe tomatoes, olive oil, garlic and basil. The pasta retains the nutty flavor of the whole grain, while the sauce adds a bright sweet‑tart note.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain pasta provides more fiber and micronutrients than traditional white pasta.
Tomato sauce is rich in lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that becomes more bioavailable after cooking.
The dish is often served in Italian restaurants as a healthier alternative to classic pasta.
The combination of whole grain and tomatoes promotes lasting satiety.
Tomatoes used in the sauce can be fresh or canned, but choose varieties without added sugar.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole grain pasta contains both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and blood‑sugar regulation.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Complex carbohydrates provide a steady release of energy and help maintain fullness.

items.title: Lycopene and antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes supply lycopene, which may reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease and certain cancers.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The pasta offers B1, B3 and folate, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Olive oil in the sauce delivers monounsaturated fats that support heart health.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Whole grain pasta contains gluten, so individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should opt for gluten‑free versions.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauce can be salty; monitor added salt to keep sodium intake in check.

items.title: Acidity of tomatoes
items.content: People with gastritis or reflux may experience discomfort from the acidic sauce.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, mixed with the sauce. Top with grated Parmesan, fresh basil, or olives. For a lighter option, use egg‑free whole grain pasta.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry pasta in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked sauce keeps in the refrigerator for up to 3 days, and the prepared dish should be consumed within 2 days.

potato-french-fries-ns-as-to-fresh-or-fr.title: Potato, French Fries, Fresh or Frozen

content.title: About
content.content: French fries are thin strips of potato that are deep‑fried or baked until golden and crisp. The product is available either fresh (raw, ready to be cooked) or frozen (blanched and quick‑frozen for long‑term storage).

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: French fries originated in Belgium in the late 19th century and quickly spread worldwide.
Frozen fries allow the taste and crunch to be retained even after extended storage.
A double‑fry method (low temperature first, then high) is often used to achieve a perfect golden crust.
There are many variants: classic, seasoned, sweet potato, and cheese‑covered fries.
In the United States, fries are one of the most consumed side dishes.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, which supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Fresh potatoes contain vitamin C, an antioxidant that boosts immunity.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Keeping the skin and using whole pieces preserves fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Low sodium when prepared without added salt
items.content: If no salt is added during cooking, fries can be a moderate‑sodium side.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Potatoes provide quick energy through their carbohydrate content.

items.title: High fat content when deep‑fried
items.content: Traditional deep‑frying adds significant amounts of saturated and trans fats.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: French fries are calorie‑dense; portion control is important, especially on weight‑loss diets.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: High‑temperature cooking can produce acrylamide, a potential toxin with frequent consumption.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to potatoes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve fries hot as a side to meat dishes, in burgers, or as a snack. Sprinkle with salt, spices, cheese, or herbs. Frozen fries are convenient to bake in an oven or air‑fryer without added oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh cut potatoes should be kept in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Frozen fries store in a freezer at –18 °C for up to 12 months. No thawing is required before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken stew is a dish made from pieces of chicken meat slowly simmered in broth with vegetables and spices. The meat becomes tender and the flavorful sauce turns rich and aromatic.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Stewing retains more nutrients compared with frying.
Traditional recipes around the world use different spices: in Russia – bay leaf and black pepper, in India – curry and turmeric.
Chicken is high in protein, and slow cooking makes it easier to digest.
Chicken stew is often served with a side of potatoes, rice, or grains.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken provides all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When using lean cuts (e.g., breast) and removing the skin, the dish contains little saturated fat.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken stew supplies vitamin B6, which supports metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It contains phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones and immunity.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The broth retains moisture, helping maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Food poisoning risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor pathogens such as Salmonella.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared broth often contains high salt levels; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Chicken protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken meat.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chicken stew can be served hot as a main course, added to salads, sandwiches, or used as a filling for pies. The broth can also serve as a base for soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the stew to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in portioned bags for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly before consuming.

yogurt-low-fat-milk-flavors-other-than-f.title: Yogurt, low fat milk, non‑fruit flavors

content.title: About
content.content: Yogurt made from low‑fat milk is a fermented dairy product created by adding live cultures Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus to skim milk. Non‑fruit flavors include classic, vanilla, creamy, spiced (e.g., cinnamon) and other aromatics without fruit additives.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Low‑fat yogurt retains most of milk’s nutrients while having reduced fat content.
Live cultures support gut health by improving intestinal microbiota.
Non‑fruit versions are often chosen by people monitoring sugar intake because they tend to be less sweet.
Yogurt can replace sour cream in recipes, lowering calorie density.
Fermentation of milk into yogurt originated in Central Asia over 5,000 years ago.

items.title: Rich in probiotics
items.content: Live bacteria help maintain a balanced gut microbiome, aiding digestion and immunity.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Low‑fat yogurt provides about 10 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The reduced‑fat profile makes it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Calcium strengthens bones and teeth and is essential for muscle function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Yogurt supplies vitamin B12 and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort, although fermentation reduces lactose levels.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein or whey requires complete avoidance of the product.

items.title: Added sugar content
items.content: Some flavored varieties may contain hidden sugars; check the label.

items.title: Probiotic spoilage
items.content: Improper storage can kill beneficial cultures and allow pathogenic growth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy yogurt as a snack, blend into smoothies, use in sauces, dressings, baked goods, or as a base for dips. Non‑fruit flavors pair well with nuts, honey, whole grains and spices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store yogurt in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C in its original container. After opening, consume within 5‑7 days. Do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.
